# Feelings in full {#feelings}

## The gap {#gap}

*I'm always anxious* makes a mood that has settled in sound like who you are, and *for a second I was furious* is soon remembered as plain fury. *I'm scared it'll go wrong* sounds as if the danger is already here, when it may never come. Ageben says how long a feeling lasts and whether its cause is real or only predicted, and it adds six more urges, such as freezing or keeping the peace.

## The forms {#forms}
<!-- Agent summary: extends the feeling word from What a feeling wants (thanks/sorry word + urge vowel + last ending) in three ways: six more urges, a meaning for the last ending (how long the feeling lasts), and `thomam` before the word for a cost that may come. Parts (table): `thuna` autonomy, `thu` unmet, middle `m` (the thanks/sorry ending: how lasting the harm is; `-m` = can still change), `uo` push back, last `l` settled in. Placement unchanged: after the English clause the feeling is about. -->

In *What a feeling wants*, you built a feeling word from a thanks or sorry word, which names a sake (the need involved) and says whether it was met. After it come one vowel for the urge, which is what the feeling makes you want to do, and a last `-m`. This lesson adds three things to that word: six more urges, a meaning for the last ending, and a way to say that a cost has not come yet.

Here is a feeling word that uses two of the additions, read from left to right:

| `thuna` | `thu` | `m` | `uo` | `l` |
|---------|-------|-----|------|-----|
| autonomy | unmet | default ending | push back (urge) | settled in (how long) |

`thuna` names the sake autonomy, your say in what you do, and `thu` says it went unmet. The `m` after it is the ending from *Thanks and sorry*, which on a sorry word says how lasting the harm is. At the default `-m`, the harm could still change. Then come `uo`, one of the new urges, which means *push back*, and a last `-l`, which says the feeling has settled in. So `thunathumuol` says *my say was taken, I want to push back, and the feeling has settled in*.

The feeling word goes where it went in *What a feeling wants*: after the English clause the feeling is about, as in *He rewrote my memo again `thunathumuol`*.

## Six more urges {#urges}
<!-- Agent summary: six two-vowel urges (table), in the same place as `a` `e` `o` `u`; they name pulls those four blur together. Small English words: `oe` toward, `uo` against, `ua` out of, `ao` using, `ae` on, `ue` through. `oe` `uo` `ua` `ao` move you in relation to someone (like `e` `o` `u`); `ae` `ue` point at no one (like `a`). `oe`: met sake = want to tell someone, unmet = want someone with you. No urge is the right one to have. Two mix → name the stronger, or use two feeling words to say both. -->

The four urges from *What a feeling wants* are one vowel each: stay in it, act on someone, do something for someone, and move off. Six more urges are two vowels each, and they go in the same place in the word. They name pulls that the first four blur together, such as freezing in place or calming someone down to stay safe.

| Urge | Goes with | It makes you want to | Belongs when |
|------|-----------|----------------------|--------------|
| `oe` | *toward* | turn to someone: for comfort, or to share it | company would help, or you have good news to tell |
| `uo` | *against* | push back on an outcome or a demand | a limit is being crossed |
| `ua` | *out of* | step out of the fight: let go, yield | it can't be changed, or it isn't worth the cost |
| `ao` | *using* | use yourself to keep the peace | calming things down keeps someone safe |
| `ae` | *on* | stay on the spot: frozen, or keeping a lid on it | acting now would cost more than waiting |
| `ue` | *through* | do something, but you can't tell what | you don't know yet |

Each of the first four urges goes with a small English word: `a` with *in*, `e` with *at*, `o` with *for*, and `u` with *from*. The new urges follow the same pattern. With `oe` you turn *toward* someone, and with `uo` you push *against* something. `ua` takes you *out of* the fight, and with `ao` you keep the peace *using* yourself. `ae` keeps you *on* the spot, or keeps a lid *on* the feeling, and with `ue` the feeling runs *through* you and you can't tell which way it pulls.

The ten urges also fall into two groups. `oe`, `uo`, `ua`, and `ao` move you in relation to someone, as `e`, `o`, and `u` do. `ae` and `ue` point at no one, as `a` does, because holding still and not knowing which way to go are not aimed at anybody.

The same event can bring either of two new urges:

> He rewrote my memo again `thunathumuom`.  
> He rewrote my memo again `thunathumuam`.

Both say your say was taken. With `uo`, you want to push back on the rewrite, which fits when a limit is being crossed. With `ua`, you want to step out of the fight and let the memo go, which fits when a fight over it isn't worth the cost.

The urge `oe` covers two pulls toward someone, and the sake word says which one:

> The exam results came in `thuwathamoem`.  
> The exam results came in `thuwathumoem`.

With `tha`, your competence was met, so you want to tell someone the news. With `thu`, it went unmet, so you want someone with you.

As with the first four, no urge is the right one to have, and the *Belongs when* column names some times when each one fits. When two urges mix, name the stronger one, or use two feeling words to say both.

## How long the feeling lasts {#duration}
<!-- Agent summary: last ending = how long the feeling itself lasts: `-l` settled in (hours, days, a mood), `-m` (default) left open, `-r` a flash or a wave that will pass. Same direction as How sure are you? (`-l` ≈ lasting, `-r` ≈ right now). `-r` → a feeling you can wait out; `-l` → a feeling that needs attention of its own. Can't tell how long: `-l` and `-r` say more than you know; `-m` says nothing about it. -->

The last letter of a feeling word is its ending, and it says how long the feeling itself lasts. These are the three endings from *How sure are you?*, where you could think of `-l` as *lasting* and `-r` as *right now*. They run in the same direction here.

| Ending | The feeling |
|--------|-------------|
| `-l` | has settled in for hours or days, as a mood |
| `-m` | lasts for a time the word leaves open (the default) |
| `-r` | comes as a flash or a wave, and will pass |

Here is the same feeling with each end of the scale:

> He rewrote my memo again `thunathumuol`.  
> He rewrote my memo again `thunathumuor`.

Both say your say was taken and you want to push back. With `-l`, the feeling has settled in, and it may last for days. With `-r`, it is a wave that will pass. That difference suggests what to do next, because a feeling marked `-r` is one you can wait out, and a feeling marked `-l` needs attention of its own.

When you can't tell how long the feeling will last, `-l` and `-r` each say more than you know, and `-m` says nothing about how long.

## A cost that may come {#may-come}
<!-- Agent summary: a feeling word alone says its cost or payoff is real. For fear, worry, or hope about what hasn't happened, put `thomam` (could be) right before the feeling word: the event may cost you or pay off. `thomam` keeps its endings: `thomal` adds that you'll find out whether the cost is real. Omit `thomam` when the cost or payoff has happened. -->

A feeling word on its own says that the cost or payoff it names is real. Fear, worry, and hope are about something that has not happened yet. For those, put `thomam` right before the feeling word. It is the *could be* word from *How sure are you?*, and here it says that the event may cost you something or pay off, without saying that it has.

> My boss raised his voice `thobathumaor`.  
> My boss raised his voice `thomam thobathumaor`.

The first sentence says you are in danger. The second says only that you may be. In both, you want to calm him down, and the feeling is a flash. So you can say you are afraid without saying the danger is here.

`thomam` keeps the endings it has in *How sure are you?*, where the ending says what you will do about a guess. For example, `thomal thobathumaor` adds that you will find out whether the danger is real. When the cost or payoff has already happened, leave `thomam` out.

## Examples {#examples}

> The review is tomorrow `thomam thuwathumur`.  
> He rewrote my memo again `thunathumuol`.  
> We stopped speaking years ago `thawethuluar`.  
> My boss raised his voice `thomam thobathumaor`.  
> The deadline moved up `thuwathumael`.

| Drop-in | What it says | Instead of | The parts |
|---------|--------------|------------|-----------|
| `thuwathumur` | it may cost me competence, and I want to get away; a wave | *anxious* | competence unmet; move off; a wave |
| `thunathumuol` | my say was taken, and I want to push back; it has settled in | *resentful* | autonomy unmet; push back; settled in |
| `thawethuluar` | a wave of grief over a loss that stays | *sad* | relatedness unmet for good; let go; a wave |
| `thobathumaor` | I may be in danger, and I want to calm him down; a flash | *scared* | physical unmet; keep the peace; a flash |
| `thuwathumael` | I can't keep up, and I'm frozen; it has settled in | *overwhelmed* | competence unmet; stay on the spot; settled in |

In the review sentence, `thomam` says the review may cost you competence, so the sentence does not say it has gone badly, and `-r` says the wish to get away will pass. `thawethuluar` pairs a loss that is for good with a feeling that comes and goes. `thobathumaor` names the urge to calm your boss down before you follow it, so you can still choose whether to follow it.

## Telling the parts apart {#telling-apart}
<!-- Agent summary: near misses. `a` = no pull; `ae` = a pull, holding still; `ue` = a pull, direction unknown. Middle ending = the situation (sorry word: `-l` for good, `-m` can still change, `-r` passed); last ending = the feeling; when they disagree (settled feeling over a passed cost) the feeling no longer matches the situation. Last ending = how long, never how strong: a strong flash takes `-r`, a mild lasting feeling `-l`. -->

Three parts of a feeling word are easily confused, and each pair is told apart differently.

### Three ways to stay put {#staying-put}

The urges `a`, `ae`, and `ue` all leave you where you are, for different reasons:

> The deadline moved up `thuwathumam`.  
> The deadline moved up `thuwathumaem`.  
> The deadline moved up `thuwathumuem`.

All three say the new deadline costs you competence. With `a`, nothing pulls you to move, and you sit with the feeling. With `ae`, something pulls you, and you are holding still: frozen, or keeping a lid on it. With `ue`, something pulls you, and you can't tell which way yet. So when something pulls you and you can't say which way, the urge is `ue`.

### The situation or the feeling {#situation-or-feeling}

A feeling word has two endings, and they are about different things. The middle one is the ending of the sorry word, and it describes the situation: `-l` says the cost is for good, `-m` says it could still change, and `-r` says it has passed. The last one describes the feeling, and says how long it lasts.

> We stopped speaking years ago `thawethulual`.  
> We stopped speaking years ago `thawethuluar`.  
> We made up last week `thawethurual`.

All three pair unmet connection with `ua`, the urge to let go. In the first two the loss is for good. With `thawethulual` the grief has settled in as well, and with `thawethuluar` it comes in waves. In the third, the middle `-r` says the cost has passed, and the last `-l` says the feeling has not. When the two endings disagree like this, the feeling no longer matches the situation, which is a reason to look at it again.

### How long or how strong {#long-or-strong}

The last ending says how long a feeling lasts and nothing about how strong it is. A strong feeling can pass in a moment, and a mild one can stay for days.

> For a second I was furious `thunathumuor`.  
> I've been a little irritated all week `thunathumuol`.

The fury was strong and lasted a second, so its ending is `-r`. The irritation is mild and has lasted all week, so its ending is `-l`.

## Practice {#practice}

Build the feeling word from the parts in the note.

**1.** *I passed the exam.* (competence met, default ending; I want to tell someone; a flash)

::: details Show answer
I passed the exam `thuwathamoer`.
:::

**2.** *The biopsy results come Friday.* (it may cost my health, and that can still change; I can't tell which way it pulls; it has settled in)

::: details Show answer
The biopsy results come Friday `thomam thobathumuel`.
:::

**3.** *We made up last week.* (connection unmet, but the cost has passed; I'm still pushing back; it has settled in)

::: details Show answer
We made up last week `thawethuruol`.
:::

**4.** *We made up last week.* (connection unmet, but the cost has passed; I'm still pushing back; a wave that will pass)

::: details Show answer
We made up last week `thawethuruor`.
:::

**5.** *My boss raised his voice.* (I'm in danger, and that can still change; I want to calm him down; a flash)

::: details Show answer
My boss raised his voice `thobathumaor`.
:::

**6.** *My boss raised his voice.* (I may be in danger, and that can still change; I want to calm him down; a flash)

::: details Show answer
My boss raised his voice `thomam thobathumaor`.
:::

**7.** *The deadline moved up.* (I can't keep up, and that can still change; I'm frozen; it has settled in)

::: details Show answer
The deadline moved up `thuwathumael`.
:::

**8.** *The deadline moved up.* (I can't keep up, and that can still change; something pulls me, but I can't tell which way; it has settled in)

::: details Show answer
The deadline moved up `thuwathumuel`.
:::
